newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Pilots' bid to save time caused Colombia air crash.
newsitem.headline: Pilots' bid to save time caused Colombia air crash.

text.p: Pilots were trying to save 12 minutes flying time when their American Airlines jet crashed into a mountain in Colombia last December, killing 167 people aboard, crash investigators said on Monday.

In an effort to replot the Boeing 757's approach to Cali airport in southwest Colombia, the co-pilot punched an incorrect code into the flight computer, which, combined with other human errors, caused the craft to veer left and slam into mountains, the accident report said.

Flight 965 had left Miami one hour 40 minutes late and the plane's captain was worried his crew would not have sufficient time to rest in Cali before returning to the United States, Capt. Rodrigo Cabrera of Colombia's civil aviation authority told a news conference.

"Cali airport was congested and the crew's wish to avoid any delays in landing could have been a contributing factor. Opting to land on a different runway would have saved them approximately 12 minutes," he said.

As a matter of routine Colombian flight controllers offered the American Airlines crew the option of landing on a different runway to the one originally scheduled when it was still 63 miles (101 km) out.
But Cabrera said that would have been insufficient time to replot the approach unless the crew had previously entered the alternative coordinates into the aircraft computer.

In the official accident report, released in Washington on Friday and in Colombia on Monday, the pilots were severely criticised for not switching from computer to radio navigation when they realised they were off course. The Colombian airport authorities were cleared of blame.
Cabrera described the American Airlines crews as generally "very well disciplined" but said the pilots had tried to verify their exact location in an "unorthodox fashion."
"You must understand that moments of stress can lead to situations like this," he said.
Just five people and a dog survived the impact when the aircraft crashed in a remote area near the town of Buga.
Tragedy could have been averted if the pilots had suspended their descent from 23,000 feet (7,010 meters) when they realised they were off course, Cabrera said.

He said that the pilot's failure to release the jet's speed brakes as he made a last-ditch effort to avoid ploughing into a mountain in the rebel-infested Buga area, just outside Cali, contributed to the fatal crash.

Shortly after the crash it was revealed that the airport's radar had not been functioning since it was destroyed by leftist guerrillas four years earlier. But Cabrera said on Monday that the equipment was for monitoring flight paths and would have been unable to track an aircraft's final approach.
